triage.name: Minimal change disease
triage.reason: Sudden nephrotic syndrome with edema and proteinuria, especially in children; diagnosis by history, labs and biopsy, with other nephrotic syndromes as look-alikes.

demographics: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, accounting for the majority of cases in that age group
In adults it accounts for a minority of nephrotic syndrome cases and is more often secondary to another condition or drug

risk_factors.text: Recent upper respiratory infection or other viral illness
Use of NSAIDs or other implicated medications

chief_complaints.text: My child's face and eyes are puffy, especially in the morning
My child's legs and ankles are swollen
My child has gained weight quickly
My child seems tired and less active

hpi.onset: Gradual over days to a few weeks; often noticed first as puffiness around the eyes in the morning
hpi.progression: Edema worsens over days, spreading from the face to the legs, abdomen and genitals; weight rises steadily; urine becomes frothy
hpi.location: Periorbital and facial swelling early, then dependent edema of the legs, abdominal distension and scrotal or vulvar swelling
hpi.quality: Soft, pitting swelling that shifts with position; worse in the morning around the eyes and worse in the legs later in the day
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at first, becoming marked; weight gain of several pounds over days
hpi.timing: Periorbital edema worst on waking; leg edema worse after standing or at the end of the day
aggravating: Standing or sitting upright for long periods

associated_symptoms.text: Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing

pertinent_negatives: Weight loss, night sweats or fever
Use of NSAIDs or other implicated medications

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, abdominal pain or scrotal swelling rather than reporting edema; parents often notice puffy eyes or frothy urine first.

Adults more often have a secondary cause (NSAIDs, malignancy, infection) and may present with less dramatic edema but more fatigue and weight gain; hypertension and hematuria are still uncommon but more likely than in children.
missing_classic_features: Periorbital edema as the sole initial finding

atypical.how_it_differs: Edema is common in normal pregnancy, so new-onset proteinuria and hypertension must be distinguished from preeclampsia; minimal change disease is rare in pregnancy.
missing_classic_features: Periorbital edema as an isolated finding

general.mild: Well-appearing, puffy around the eyes in the morning, playful
general.moderate: Puffy face and swollen legs, moving more slowly, clothes and shoes feel tight
general.severe: Markedly swollen face, abdomen and legs, uncomfortable, prefers to lie down
general.critical: Ill-appearing, grossly edematous, lethargic or in respiratory distress

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and around the eyes, especially in the morning
findings.finding: Puffy, boggy periorbital and facial swelling

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the shins and ankles for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities, graded 1+ to 4+

findings.maneuver: Percuss the flanks for dullness and test for shifting dullness or a fluid wave
findings.finding: Dullness in the flanks that shifts with position, consistent with ascites

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scrotum (or vulva) with the patient's permission
Weigh the patient and compare with a recent weight
findings.finding: Rapid weight gain of several pounds over days

findings.maneuver: Measure the blood pressure with an appropriately sized cuff
findings.finding: Blood pressure within the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the trunk, limbs and pressure areas
Inspect and palpate the joints of the hands, wrists, knees and ankles
findings.finding: No joint swelling, warmth or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 30–45 degrees
Auscultate the lung fields posteriorly and at the bases
Percuss and palpate the liver edge

labs.caveat: Dipstick detects albumin well; a negative dipstick makes nephrotic-range proteinuria very unlikely.
Hypoalbuminemia is the key driver of edema and of the low measured total calcium.
Hyperlipidemia is part of the nephrotic syndrome and reverses with remission.
Creatinine is often normal; a rise suggests hypovolemia, acute kidney injury or a different glomerular disease.
Dilutional hyponatremia from water retention; true sodium deficit is uncommon.
Low total calcium tracks the low albumin; ionized calcium is usually normal.
Microscopic hematuria is absent or minimal; more than a few red cells per high-power field points away from minimal change disease.
Fatty casts or oval fat bodies support nephrotic-range proteinuria but are not specific to minimal change disease.
Thyroid-binding globulin is lost in the urine, so TSH may rise; usually not clinically significant.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or immunosuppressive therapy.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging in children and in anyone with suspected renal vein thrombosis

findings.text: Absent or reversed flow in a renal vein (renal vein thrombosis)

initial.why: Shows heavy proteinuria with little or no blood or leukocytes, the hallmark of nephrotic syndrome
Hypoalbuminemia supports nephrotic syndrome and explains the edema
Baseline kidney function, sodium and potassium before treatment
Baseline blood counts; anemia or thrombocytosis may reflect the nephrotic state
Hyperlipidemia is part of the nephrotic syndrome
Rules out pregnancy before biopsy, imaging or immunosuppression

confirmatory.test: Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis: normal light microscopy, no immune deposits, and diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy

supporting.why: Confirms two kidneys, excludes obstruction or structural disease, and screens for renal vein thrombosis
supporting.only_if: atypical features, suspected thrombosis or before biopsy

supporting.why: Thyroid-binding globulin loss can raise TSH; check if symptoms suggest thyroid disease
Screens for an underlying infection or inflammatory process
supporting.only_if: fever or other signs of infection

supporting.why: Screens for an underlying inflammatory or malignant process
supporting.only_if: adult with weight loss, night sweats or other systemic symptoms

supporting.why: Evaluates pleural effusions or pulmonary edema
supporting.only_if: dyspnea, hypoxemia or abnormal lung exam

not_indicated.why: Not needed in a typical child with classic nephrotic syndrome who responds to steroids
Not routine; only for respiratory symptoms
Not routine in the absence of infection
Not routine in children with classic presentation
No role in nephrotic syndrome; renal vein thrombosis is assessed by Doppler ultrasound or CT
Not indicated unless sepsis is suspected

decision_points: Confirm nephrotic-range proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia before considering biopsy
Biopsy is generally not required in a child aged 1–10 with classic nephrotic syndrome who responds to corticosteroids

Biopsy is indicated in adults, in children under 1 or over 10, in steroid-resistant cases, or when features suggest another glomerular disease (hypertension, hematuria, low complement, systemic symptoms)
Pregnancy test before biopsy or immunosuppressive therapy in anyone who could be pregnant
Screen for renal vein thrombosis if flank pain, hematuria or a sudden decline in kidney function occurs

criteria.name: Nephrotic syndrome
criteria.summary: Nephrotic-range proteinuria (generally >3.5 g per day in adults or >40 mg/m² per hour in children) plus hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia.

criteria.name: Minimal change disease on biopsy
criteria.summary: Normal glomeruli on light microscopy, no immune deposits on immunofluorescence, and diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy.
items: Diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy

differential.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
differential.why_considered: The most important look-alike: same nephrotic syndrome with edema, heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia, and it can only be told apart from minimal change disease on biopsy.
differential.trigger: Nephrotic syndrome that does not remit with a course of corticosteroids, or an adult with nephrotic syndrome and reduced kidney function

history: More common in adults and in Black patients
Higher rates of progression to chronic kidney disease
May be secondary to HIV, obesity, or heroin use
exam: Hypertension more frequent than in minimal change disease
Edema similar in distribution to minimal change disease
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show smaller, echogenic kidneys in chronic cases

differential.name: Membranous nephropathy
differential.why_considered: A common cause of adult nephrotic syndrome with identical edema and proteinuria, distinguished by biopsy and serology.
differential.trigger: Adult with nephrotic syndrome, especially with a history of malignancy, hepatitis B, or autoimmune disease

history: May be associated with solid tumors, hepatitis B, or lupus
exam: Edema similar to minimal change disease
labs: Complement may be low if associated with lupus
imaging: Renal ultrasound to exclude structural disease

differential.name: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis
differential.why_considered: Can present with edema and proteinuria in a child after a recent infection, but the urinary findings and course differ.

history: Recent sore throat or impetigo 1–3 weeks earlier
exam: Periorbital edema but often with hematuria
Rash or joint findings if systemic
labs: Active urinary sediment with red blood cells and red cell casts
Elevated antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B titers
imaging: Renal ultrasound usually normal or mildly enlarged kidneys

differential.name: IgA nephropathy
differential.why_considered: A common glomerulonephritis that can cause proteinuria and edema, though nephrotic-range proteinuria is less typical.

history: Gross hematuria during or shortly after an upper respiratory infection
Recurrent episodes of visible blood in urine
Normal blood pressure or mild hypertension
exam: Usually no significant edema unless nephrotic-range proteinuria develops
labs: Active urinary sediment with red blood cells and red cell casts

differential.name: Lupus nephritis
differential.why_considered: Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause nephrotic syndrome with edema and proteinuria, especially in young women.
differential.trigger: Nephrotic syndrome with rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, or other systemic features

labs: Positive antinuclear antibody and anti-double-stranded DNA
imaging: Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and exclude other causes

differential.name: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)
differential.why_considered: A small-vessel vasculitis that can cause nephrotic-range proteinuria and edema in children.

history: Palpable purpura on the buttocks and lower legs
labs: Active urinary sediment with red blood cells

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Causes edema and weight gain, but the distribution and associated findings differ from nephrotic syndrome.

exam: Edema that is symmetric and dependent
labs: Urine dipstick negative or trace for protein
imaging: Chest x-ray showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema
Echocardiogram showing reduced ejection fraction or structural disease

differential.name: Cirrhosis
differential.why_considered: Causes hypoalbuminemia, edema and ascites, which can mimic nephrotic syndrome.

history: Known liver disease or risk factors (alcohol, hepatitis)
labs: Urine dipstick negative or trace for protein
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound showing nodular liver, splenomegaly, and ascites

severity.mild: Early nephrotic syndrome: periorbital puffiness and mild leg edema, weight gain of a few pounds, normal blood pressure, normal kidney function, proteinuria present but not yet massive.
severity.moderate: Established nephrotic syndrome: marked periorbital and lower extremity edema, abdominal distension, foamy urine, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, possibly mild hyponatremia or hypokalemia; blood pressure and creatinine still normal.
severity.severe: Severe nephrotic syndrome: gross anasarca, scrotal or vulvar edema, ascites, pleural effusions, dyspnea, profound hypoalbuminemia, and risk of infection or thrombosis; may have acute kidney injury from hypovolemia.
severity.critical: Life-threatening complications: sepsis, extensive venous thrombosis (including renal vein thrombosis), respiratory failure from massive edema or pleural effusions, or acute kidney injury requiring dialysis.

red_flags.finding: Fever, abdominal pain, or diffuse tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or sepsis; nephrotic patients are immunosuppressed from urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement.

red_flags.finding: Sudden flank pain, gross hematuria, or rapid decline in kidney function
red_flags.meaning: Renal vein thrombosis; requires urgent imaging with Doppler ultrasound or CT.

red_flags.finding: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, or hypoxemia
red_flags.meaning: Pulmonary embolism or pleural effusion; nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state.

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain, distension, or absent bowel sounds
red_flags.meaning: Possible bowel ischemia or perforation from severe edema or thrombosis.
Hypovolemia from aggressive diuresis or sepsis; may precipitate acute kidney injury.
Severe hyponatremia, hypertensive encephalopathy, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

complications.name: Infection (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, cellulitis, pneumonia, sepsis)
clues: Positive blood or ascitic fluid cultures

complications.name: Venous thromboembolism (renal vein thrombosis, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism)
Malnutrition and growth failure
clues: Weight loss or failure to gain weight

complications.name: Steroid toxicity (growth suppression, cataracts, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension)
Relapse of nephrotic syndrome
clues: Return of edema and foamy urine
Often triggered by infection or steroid taper

special_populations.differences: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children; typically responds rapidly to corticosteroids, but relapses are common. Growth and development must be monitored during steroid therapy.
More likely to have a secondary cause (NSAIDs, malignancy, infection) and to require biopsy. Steroid side effects are more severe; bone protection and glucose monitoring are important.
Rare; edema and proteinuria must be distinguished from preeclampsia. Hypertension and elevated liver enzymes favor preeclampsia. Management requires close collaboration with obstetrics.
Higher risk of severe infections; live vaccines are contraindicated. Immunosuppressive therapy requires careful monitoring.
Creatinine may rise from hypovolemia or acute kidney injury; diuresis must be cautious. Biopsy is often needed to exclude other glomerular diseases.

key_questions.question: When did the swelling start, and where did you first notice it?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to a few weeks, starting around the eyes in the morning, then spreading to the legs and abdomen

key_questions.question: Is the puffiness worse in the morning or at the end of the day?
key_questions.looking_for: Periorbital swelling worst on waking; leg swelling worse after standing

key_questions.question: Have you noticed that the urine looks foamy or frothy?
Has there been any blood in the urine, or urine that looks cola-colored?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; gross hematuria points away from minimal change disease toward a nephritic process

key_questions.question: Has the child gained weight recently, or do clothes and shoes feel tight?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapid weight gain of several pounds over days from fluid retention

key_questions.question: Has there been a recent cold, sore throat, or other viral illness?
key_questions.looking_for: A recent upper respiratory infection is a common trigger

key_questions.question: Does the child have any known allergies, asthma, or eczema?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopic disease is weakly associated with minimal change disease

key_questions.question: Has the child taken any ibuprofen, naproxen, or other anti-inflammatory medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAID use can cause secondary minimal change disease; stopping the drug may resolve it

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of kidney disease or nephrotic syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; a strong family history suggests an inherited or alternative glomerular disease

key_questions.question: Has the child had any fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, or joint pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these features suggest systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, or malignancy rather than minimal change disease

key_questions.question: Has the child had any trouble breathing, chest pain, or a swollen, painful leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, or unilateral leg swelling suggesting venous thromboembolism, a known complication of nephrotic syndrome

key_questions.question: Has the child had any severe abdominal pain, fever, or been more sleepy or confused than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, sepsis, or severe hyponatremia; nephrotic patients are immunosuppressed

reasoning_points: Nephrotic syndrome is present: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia
The presentation is classic for a child aged 2–6 with periorbital edema, foamy urine, and rapid weight gain after a viral illness
Blood pressure is normal and there is no gross hematuria, rash, or joint involvement, arguing against a nephritic or systemic process
Urinalysis shows heavy protein with little or no blood or leukocytes, and no red cell casts
Renal function is typically normal or only mildly reduced
Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and usually responds rapidly to corticosteroids
Biopsy is not required in a typical child who responds to steroids; it is indicated in adults, in children under 1 or over 10, or when features suggest another glomerular disease
Complications to consider include infection, venous thromboembolism including renal vein thrombosis, and acute kidney injury

easy: Child aged 2–6 with periorbital edema, foamy urine, and rapid weight gain
Recent upper respiratory infection as a trigger
Normal blood pressure and no hematuria
Urinalysis with heavy protein and no active sediment
medium: Older child or adolescent with nephrotic syndrome, where focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a stronger consideration
Adult with new nephrotic syndrome and a history of NSAID use
Mild microscopic hematuria or mildly elevated creatinine that raises concern for another glomerular disease
Scrotal or vulvar edema and abdominal distension as the presenting complaint rather than facial swelling
hard: Nephrotic syndrome that does not remit after a course of corticosteroids, suggesting focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Adult with nephrotic syndrome and systemic features such as rash or joint pain, suggesting lupus nephritis
Child with nephrotic syndrome and sudden flank pain or gross hematuria from renal vein thrombosis
Patient presenting with fever and abdominal pain from spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as the first clue to nephrotic syndrome
Pregnant patient with edema and proteinuria, where preeclampsia must be excluded
